utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simunovic, what were the forces that you had in Dubrovnik in fact, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean military units?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean men under arms. As you yourself said, you had policemen and civilians and members of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and members of the National Guards Corps and members of the special police, members of the Territorial Defence, at the beginning of the aggression on Dubrovnik, there were between 650 and 700 men in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some people said here that there were a hundred, 200, 300. Now we see Nojko Marinovic mentioning the figure of 670. Maybe you heard when your predecessor, that is, Mr. Kriste, who was Minister of Defence at the time, spoke here and said that at meetings with representatives of the JNA you claimed you had 5.000 to sort of trick them. In your opinion, how were they able to establish how many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We actually believed that the Yugoslav army had information. I don't know about the statements of the witnesses who appeared before me, but I can state emphatically what I do know, and what I have told you are correct figures. It's another matter that the Yugoslav army wanted to give the impression that Dubrovnik was full of all kinds of armed forces. But at these joint meetings that we had, we denied all that, and I believe that you too are familiar with this and that this was conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was nothing they had to convey to me. I was the President of Serbia and was not involved in that. But from the information I have, were there people from the outside, people from abroad there?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that there were no military operations in the old town, and you claim that emphatically.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our part, there were no operations, but on your part there were plenty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a unit that was supposed to act in the old town, did you not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were units that were formed before the actual beginning of the aggression. These were the units of the so-called local communities. However, as the old town, or the monument, protected monument of the old town had a local community of its own and it was entitled to form such a unit. However, when the unit was formed, I personally disbanded it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you disbanded it but the unit had been formed?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as it had been in all local communities. They were so-called national protection detachments, their primary aim being to protect the inhabitants of those local communities in the event of aggression. This was even before the aggression began against the town of Dubrovnik. When I say the town of Dubrovnik, I mean the Dubrovnik municipality in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those sandbags that we saw, were they linked to the existence of that unit in the old town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Mr. Accused, that you who yesterday showed so much knowledge linked to artillery, being a reserve officer of the former army, you must know that those sandbags were used exclusively to protect monuments of culture. The stone plasterworks. Unfortunately, we didn't have enough of them. If we had had enough, we would have saved more of the old town than we managed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Simunovic. Was the command of your forces in the police building that was in the very centre of Dubrovnik, at least for a time?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command was for a time in the police building, but the police building was then on Marsal Tito Road number 35, which is the same building as the one in which the state security service was stationed. And you mentioned a name yesterday which I'd rather not mention. So they were five kilometres away from the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not mention in any -- anything in any kind of statement of mine, but I asked you --

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were talking about a person who was in that same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I was referring to what you said in your own statement. I asked you to explain, and you didn't explain it because you said that there was an error in the translation or something. I asked you whether this Risto --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's not go over old ground like this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, you say: "I believe that Risto Vreca, a senior official of the DB in Dubrovnik, organised Serbian nationalist activities in town." What kind of Serbian nationalist activities did this Risto Vreca organise in town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vreca, at the time of the aggression, was already retired. However, that same gentleman and his service provided security for you in the period prior to 1989. He had close contacts vertically with his superiors and as far as we know - but I will limit myself to the municipality of Dubrovnik - we do know that such links existed and that such cooperation existed along the change of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That there were links with the state security along the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that better than I do probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know anything better than you. I'm just asking you to explain how this Risto Vreca organised Serbian nationalist activities in town. What kind of activities were they, please?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can consider the formation the individual parties, rallying on an ethnic basis, and various in camera meetings of this minority in Dubrovnik in those days, which was not in jeopardy in any sense of the term, then one could probably conclude with certainty that this gentleman was behind it as nothing could happen in Dubrovnik without him knowing it about or, rather, his service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this man retire?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means in 1990. I see. So let's clear that up at least. So he retired a year and a half before these things happened that you referred to. Let me tell you what Marinovic says on page 19 in connection with the question where your command was, and I quote: "For the first two months, my command post was in the police building. We later moved it to the Zagreb Hotel in Lapad, and in 1992 it was moved to the Splendid Hotel which was to some extent protected by the Petka hill." So this first position was not in the centre of Dubrovnik but several kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several kilometres away from the very centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not waste time on that any more. You listed meetings that you attended, and they virtually took place almost on a daily basis. And I've seen the list of meetings that you have provided, and you see -- and I see that on that list, without any exception, one of the foreign observers or mediators always attended, the people who mediated between you and the army. Does this in itself indicate that there was an effort to resolve those problems by peaceful means, the problems that existed? You met on a daily basis without any military operations.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were military operations. They even lasted while we were negotiating possible cessations of hostilities on your part. The substance of our talks and the endeavour of the European Monitoring Mission was to try and prevent a conflict, that is, to try and prevent the activities of the JNA against civilian targets. Unfortunately, they were not very successful. And one has the impression that one body on behalf of the JNA conducted these talks and was in a certain sense misleading both us, the Croatian side, and the monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Simunovic -- let us clear this up: Is it true that at those meetings the army requested exclusively the surrender of weapons and the disbanding of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't request such things. It made all kinds of ultimatums. Among other things, it demanded that Dubrovnik surrender, that allegedly Kurds should leave Dubrovnik, that foreign mercenaries should leave the town, that the situation in the police force be put back to the situation as it was in 1990, and there were a number of other requests, and I believe you're familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am afraid I am not able to say I do, I'm sorry, but judging from what information I have here, they wanted weapons to be surrendered and various criminal elements to leave the town and for the town to be demilitarised, as it had been before this. Is that what the army wanted?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept your thesis and description of criminal elements. What the army requested we realised the moment we started negotiating. That means that up until the beginning of the negotiations, the army had burned down a couple of villages as Konavle, and along the coastline villages were looted and the population expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 10, you say that the army certainly forwarded information up the chain of command to Belgrade, and you make that conclusion because you were knowledgeable as an officer in reserve. Is that the only grounds that led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not the only one. My conclusion was based on the behaviour of the officers of the JNA when any decision had to be taken on their part, and I can confirm -- corroborate this with a number of examples. One of them is Cavtat. Colonel Svicevic, who did not receive authorisation for signing the document, and this shows that he was unable to decide. Or, as I spoke to a number of generals of the Yugoslav army in those days, I can just mention General Damjanovic. He didn't have authority, who was commander of the Hercegovina Corps. And General Pavlo Strugar also didn't have the authorities to sign an agreement when I was present. And that was the Avenger frigate with General Morillon and General Kriste present. So we concluded on that basis that the commanders in the area do not have the authority to sign anything or to agree to anything without the agreement from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't what you describe on page 12 in contradiction with what you say? When General Damjanovic, you say, said that the operations should cease and they had refused his order for the army to withdraw, how do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you know this. This was an operation on the ground when Minister Kouchner was with us at the negotiations. The Yugoslav army took advantage of the opportunity while we were negotiating. He was a minister of the French government, and General Damjanovic, commander of the Hercegovina Corps. The army once again tried to enter Dubrovnik, however they failed, thanks to our defensive forces. And upon the insistence of General Damjanovic that Captain Milan Zec should withdraw the army, and we were watching this on the other side of Rijeka Dubrovacka, he refused his order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please let's be rational with the time because we were told yesterday that I only have another 25 minutes for you.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain to you what you either don't know or what you want me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking you, because I saw on page 12 that this same General Damjanovic ordered the army to withdraw, but the army didn't withdraw. So what actually happened if this chain of command functioned properly, as you claim it did?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order for an attack issued by the Naval Maritime Centre Boka, Admiral Jokic, the order being to try and enter Dubrovnik while the negotiations were ongoing. However, General Damjanovic led the Hercegovina Corps, and probably the general and the admiral had not coordinated their views. And General Damjanovic was very embarrassed because of the presence of Minister Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but if you're talking about the chain of command going all the way up to Belgrade, then it should be quite the opposite. It was not for a sailor and a soldier to coordinate on the ground, but they both were supposed to carry out orders coming from Belgrade. So if you claim that the chain of command was in control of this operation in Dubrovnik, as you call it, this proves that it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're not right. I should like to give you another example, if Their Honours allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you may, but obviously quickly as you can, Mr. Simunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of December, a delegation of the Croatian government led by Minister Rudolf via an admiral, an assistant of General Kadijevic, that is Admiral Brovet in Belgrade, arranged a meeting in Cavtat for the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know what that explains.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. Let me explain. On the same day, on the 3rd, at the command post in Kupari, a decision was taken to attack Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the attack was not carried out, was it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, only one day later, so that this delegation could complete the talks and leave. And on the 6th, the attack started. So this is for certain that it couldn't have been done without Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And tell me this: Is it true - you've been talking about this on page 12 - you say that Damjanovic reacted very strongly when somebody behaved incorrectly towards you and that he protected you. Is it true that the JNA officers did in fact endeavour to protect you?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Damjanovic was quite an exceptional personality at the time, and in our private discussions prior to the meeting that took place in Mokosica, he tried to explain to me his role in all this, in the whole situation. And at the point that the Belgrade television crew turned up to make a statement, he gave a statement, and I was right next to him when he gave it. He gave quite a different statement. He mentioned the Kurds. He mentioned the Ustashas. He mentioned all the rest and that they had come to defend Dubrovnik. And at the end of the interview on television, he told me, "Mr. Simunovic, I apologise, but I had to say those things." And that was General Damjanovic, the commander of the Hercegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can't find an explanation for that, and it doesn't seem to me to be very logical, but just tell me this: Is it true that the army, throughout the time, said that it was just responding to your fire? You say this in -- on page 13, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we defended ourselves the whole time from the attacks launched by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you're talking about some fighting here. You speak about Mount Srdj, for example, which was left empty, and the army did not enter Srdj. Isn't that best proof of the fact that they had absolutely no intention of taking control of Srdj but just held you under siege in a blockade? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not so. The army on three occasions, three times, tried to take control of the Mount -- of Mount Srdj and the fortress on Mount Srdj, but it did not succeed in doing so. The fact that we were able to escape this and pull out in November from Mount Srdj, we were able to pull out for the simple reason that the commander - and we had a large number of casualties on the Bosanka platform - the commander didn't allow anybody else to be killed, any other people to lose their lives. But we returned the same night. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, you yourself are just saying that you were very astonished, that as the Srdj fortress had been left empty, that the army did not take control of it, and you explain that by saying that the army did not know that it had been left empty. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Let's not waste time. I have some information here, some facts and figures that I have received as to the number of times the Croatian paramilitary formations and units attacked the JNA and its facilities, that they did so for no cause, for no reason, and I have a whole list of questions on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over that. Mr. Milosevic, it would be helpful for us to know, if you would tell us, what was the JNA doing, shelling the old town? Or do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, from all the information that I have received, I state once again -- I tell you all once again, all the people attending this trial in this courtroom here, that Serbia had nothing to do with that operation whatsoever. And the information that I have received, I was able to see from that information that it says that the JNA exclusively responded to the shooting that it was being targeted with. Now, according to the information that I have received here, on the 12th of October, for example, you shot without any reason at the army. Then on the 13th of October, the 16th of October, the 17th of October, you opened fire without any reason at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with this. Where are you saying the fire came from, so the witness can deal with it. Are you alleging that this came from the old town on these occasions or not? You should make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to my information, the army, and you yourself said that at meetings you found it -- you said that it was just responding to your fire. So was that the case? Are these the right dates when you shot at the army for no reason at all from Dubrovnik which you had militarised previously?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So none of these dates that I quoted, and I have a full page of dates here, is correct. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you quote the date, could you quote the positions, what weapons were used to fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm saying that you shot at the army posts, and the army claims that it just responded, retaliated to your firing at them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, your information is incorrect. You have some very bad information there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have here five, ten, 20, 24, 28, 30 -- 33 dates in all on this piece of paper, ranging from the 12th of October to the 18th of December -- of May, 1992, and explanations that it was response and retaliation to the fire coming at them. And you claim that none of this is correct. Is that right, Mr. Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying. And with the Court's indulgence, I can give you examples of what the army did on the territory of the Dubrovnik municipality; everything it destroyed, how many civilians it killed, all the houses it burned. I can give you the exact dates and the villages where this took place. However, the dates you have just quoted, without any evidence and proof as to who did the shooting, who was shot at, I don't think that piece of paper is worth much. And the person that gave you that piece of paper gave you something that was quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Simunovic. Let me just ask you one more thing in this regard. I have here a photocopy, in memory of my -- of the co-fighters that were killed, is the 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army of Dubrovnik. I'm sure you know this. It is in memoriam to these soldiers killed. It has been printed and published, so you can't question the authenticity, and the first person killed on this list on the 28th of September 1991, it says Catovic Ismet Sreten. I have a piece of information here which claims that on that precise date, this person Sreten Catovic was killed. His father's name was Ismet, he was an engineer, a native of Trebinje, who had been working on the placing of mines, mines and fragmentation explosives, and that was the first victim and casualty. So this person actually died when you were laying mines and fragmentation explosive devices around Dubrovnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. If you will allow me, I can explain how Mr. Catovic lost his life. Mr. Catovic was a graduate engineer, he worked in the Ugalo Grafik factory of Dubrovnik. He was one of the first defenders of Dubrovnik. He was an engineer, as I said, a machine engineer, and he devised explosive devices in order to protect Dubrovnik. He was a constructor of explosives. However, in testing those explosive devices, he lost his own life. But he did not lose his life in the Dubrovnik county. He lost his life on the Osojnik plateau where he was testing some of the explosives devices he had devised. That is how that particular man lost his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he died of his own accord, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... on this particular point. You have now gone over the time we have allotted. You can ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, just one more question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were all tragic events, the events around Dubrovnik, and I'm sure that nobody is disputing that. But do you consider, Mr. Simunovic, that with that militarisation of Dubrovnik and by shooting at the army from Dubrovnik, you did some good?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not doing that. The witness has not agreed to those suggestions that you make. That's merely what you say. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- Your Honour Judge May, may I just make a brief explanation at this point? And I'll try to be as brief as possible today. You told me yesterday -- actually, you asked me whether I was challenging the fact that Dubrovnik had been bombed, shelled. I really do not wish to do that. That is up to you. You will decide and ascertain what happened in Dubrovnik, in and around Dubrovnik. It is my duty as an amicus curiae to indicate the material contained in the Prosecution evidence so that you can weigh up the evidence and proof when the time comes, in due course. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why, Mr. Simunovic, I should like to start off by asking you the following: Could you explain to the Court everything that happened around Mount Srdj and the Srdj fortress. Because in your statement, you said that most of the clashes around Srdj fortress took place between the 18th of November and the 18th and 13th of November, and then, later on, on the 6th of December. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber exactly -- tell us, where is Srdj located? It is above Dubrovnik. Mount Srdj and fortress Srdj is just above Dubrovnik, is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that hill, there are no civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but they were destroyed by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were those facilities?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a transmitter up there and a cable car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about people. Were any people -- did any people live there? Was it a residential area or was it an old imperial fortress which was a shelter?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the fortress was used as a tourist site and so were the facilities around there and then Croatian radio television had its transmitters there and the post office did too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nobody actually lived on Mount Srdj and the Srdj fortress.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were duty people up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In those critical times?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in normal times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of the army, of the Croatian army were up there?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on the date and the day; from 7 to 28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean people, men?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you one thing from your statement now. You gave a statement earlier on, and I'm referring to the following: You say that you had a gun, a cannon in Josip Kosor Street, Josip Kosor Street. I see. And it was 500 metres from the Lero Hotel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in your statement. It says 105-millimetre gun located by the Lero Hotel. Approximately 500 metres past the Lero Hotel on Josip Kosor Street. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- an artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't hear what's being said; there's interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness ought to have his copy of his statement if he's going to be challenged as to matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We better have a copy too. Mr. Tapuskovic, don't be too long, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement has been substantially cross-examined to by the accused, so may it be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 373, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask you for a map of Dubrovnik for me to be able to indicate the exact location of our gun and the exact location of the hotel that the gentleman has just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, various maps have been exhibited. Just refer us to one of those.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map of Dubrovnik, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You should know what the exhibit number is. It's not for somebody else to find it. Yes, Mr. Nice. Would you help us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make this one available. It's already been produced. Just to save time. It's 326, tab 13. Ms. Dicklich, as ever, on top of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Simunovic, this is on page 15 of your statement. In the English version, it is page 14, second paragraph, and the first paragraph as well. So, Mr. Simunovic, these are your very words: "I think it was a 105-millimetre gun. We put it there for two reasons: First of all, it was a relatively secluded, protected place." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the following paragraph, you say the following: "We had to concentrate our fire on our own positions at Srdj to keep the JNA from taking them. Our men there were ordered into the cellars of the imperial fortress, and we shelled all around them in an effort to stop the JNA attackers." And the last sentence: "The barrel of our one cannon was so overheated by that time that we had had to use wet towels to cool it off keep it functional." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, all that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was shooting from this gun, this cannon in town at Srdj hill?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All our materiel and resources were in the town of Dubrovnik. We defended the town of Dubrovnik and did so successfully. We were defending it from Dubrovnik. I'm not talking about the old protected area, the old town, I'm talking about Dubrovnik, the parks, the forests, but not near residential areas. So it is thanks to that that we were able to defend Srdj successfully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the Lero Hotel from the old part of town?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll show you this in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find my bearings on this map, please. May I be given a moment. Yes, the Lero Hotel and the old town. That is where they are. That means, in kilometres, there's about five kilometres between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that place, on the 6th of December, was that the only place that you shot at the JNA from?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With those weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you shoot from anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we did. We shot to defend ourselves, and that is our right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about the battery hit at Zarkovica. When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a battery, it was a truckload full of explosive devices which had been placed there in the shelter, in shelter of Zarkovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, in November.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While Dubrovnik was being shelled and rocketed, which means that we were defending ourselves against that same artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what a foreign observer said is correct -- and I received this from the Prosecutor. He said this was a significant successful operation for the Croatian defence forces when they were able to hit using their weapons the nearest artillery battery positioned on Zarkovica mountain and setting fire to the ammunitions depot there. However, some stray bullets ricocheted, which means they returned back from Zarkovica, they backfired, ricocheted around the old town and the shells fell on the Dubrovnik harbour, hitting a vessel, boat, that had not taken shelter. This was observed by a foreign observer, according to my evidence.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if this wasn't tragic, it would be ludicrous. You say Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ricocheted. I'll show you where Zarkovica was and where Dubrovnik was. So you mean this bullet ricocheted five kilometres, did it? I think the statement made by this particular gentleman - I know -- don't know who it was - he either gave that statement under some very strange circumstances or otherwise he's not familiar with warfare and does not know about any artillery shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We received this according to Rule 68. I have a copy of this and an explanation given by the witness, Paul Davidson, an observer who made a film, who made footage of that particular event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The witness has answered your question. You must move on rather than dealing with the statement at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell me this: Is it true that while the cease-fire was in force, while the truce was in force, you used this lull to arm yourselves?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no cease-fire. You, the Yugoslav side as it was called, never agreed to a cease-fire. It never signed the truce agreement, which means that throughout the area of the town of Dubrovnik or, rather, the broad Dubrovnik municipality, towards Dubrovacka, Primorje and so on, it never ceased its operations throughout the time it was there until it withdrew from the area, that is to say, until the Croatian forces advanced and liberated the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the following: You toured around these positions, this whole stretch from Montenegro to Dubrovnik, as Nojko Marinovic explained - he was the commander - was it all covered without -- with about 250 mines? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That there were 250 mines on the road, on that stretch of road?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but possibly because army units moved along that way, so in addition to those 250 mines, not a single mine - I don't know the exact number of mines - but as I say, not a single mine was activated, nor did a single one of your vehicles - I'm sorry to say "your" vehicle; you are their representative so that's why I say "you" - so not a single vehicle was destroyed by any one of these mines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as the JNA was moving, were six tanks destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the breakthrough, artillery preparations, infantry and tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all these weapons positioned, were they later withdrawn to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of November, were you in Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was happening in Herceg-Novi on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a funeral of soldiers killed on the Bosanka plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a certain amount of material that I must cover in re-examination. I want to do it in the most time efficient way possible. First can I turn to the statement of General Marinovic, and may I have just one minute in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard submissions on the admissibility of the statement of General Marinovic. We do not usually, as we've said before, admit statements. However, this matter -- this statement was used for the purpose of cross-examination. It's right that the Prosecution should be able to put that cross-examination into context because it's said that what the general says contradicts what this witness says, and the Trial Chamber should have the whole matter before it. It is, therefore, convenient that we have a copy of that, indeed, we must for that purpose of the statement. It then remains that the part, as Mr. Kay has suggested, that part only of the statement should be admitted; i.e., that part that was used for cross-examination. We do not agree with that. We think it is artificial to try and admit part but not admit the whole and may indeed be misleading if that course is followed. We will admit the whole statement, but we say immediately that it would be preferable if the witness was called so that he could be cross-examined upon his statement, and that no doubt can be considered, but meanwhile, we will admit it but with this caveat: That it has not been cross-examined and, therefore, has less weight than evidence which has been cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. To make best use of time, may we, first of all, have an exhibit number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have about four passages that I'll refer to for the purposes of putting the cross-examination in context. It would be convenient if there could be one placed on the overhead projector at the various pages to which I'll refer when reading, because it hasn't yet been provided to the interpreters, I don't think. I'm sorry about that. There may not be enough copies to go to them now, but if we put it on the overhead projector and I'm corrected when I start to read too fast, which I'm sure I will be, it won't take very long. If we could go, please, first to page 10. If we could lay it on the overhead projector, if the usher could do that. She's going to. Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The challenge is to the degree as to which Dubrovnik was revealed as a defended city by this witness's materials. In fact, in the middle of the page, and in his statement he makes this point: "After being in Dubrovnik for only a short period, I realised that the city was practically defenseless." If we can go to the bottom of the same page. Usher, if you could move -- thank you very much. Just at the bottom of that page. Further down. Right to the bottom. "The only unit in Dubrovnik which could have been considered to have been of relatively high quality at that time was the 37-man Special Police Unit which was part of the Dubrovnik police." We could now turn --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Simunovic, with those assessments set out in this statement?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12, just before -- a third of the way down. Further up. Further up. The paragraph beginning, "Altogether..." Mr. Simunovic, you've told us about three cannons that you got from the island of Korcula. This is what this witness says: "Altogether, we got four 85-millimetre cannons, two 76-millimetre anti-tank guns, two wire-guided missiles, munitions for the weapons, and six trucks. While in the Korcula barracks, we could only locate one sight for the cannons. We also were not aware of it at the time because it was dark and we were rushing to get in and out quickly, but the firing pins had been removed from all of the cannons. We discovered this the next morning. The JNA had already withdrawn all of their better equipment from the island, so these had effectively been abandoned. The 85-millimetre guns had been used as coastal artillery pieces, and they only had a range of about 15 kilometres, so the JNA pretty much considered them obsolete. For the purposes of defending Dubrovnik, though, they were perfect. With the removal of the firing pins, however, they had hoped to disable them for use by anyone else. As the first order of business, we used the manuals for the weapons (which we had also taken) to see what the firing pins should look like, and we then tried to improvise and make some of our own at the TUP metal factory. The material which we used to make them was of poor quality, though, so they only lasted for about two firings of the weapons. "I know that the equipment we had was of only limited value - particularly in light of the missing firing pins ..." Now, Mr. Simunovic, that is different as to number and arguably different as to number of firings, by one, from your evidence. What do you say? Do you accept what's said here or challenge it or what?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't challenge this. General Marinovic certainly had better insight regarding the condition of the equipment and the weapons, and all that is said in this statement is correct. I don't know what you meant regarding the use of those weapons, but these firing pins could not be used more than twice, as is stated here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 16, the last but one, I think, of references I'll make on detail in the statement, where again it's suggested effectively that the general reveals some kind of equality of forces. It's right, isn't it, Mr. Simunovic, that this general had come straight from the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Marinovic arrived from Trebinje where he had been the commander of the garrison in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the top of page 16. Further up. Right at the top. Thank you. "The total troop strength of the Yugoslav army forces dedicated to the Dubrovnik campaign was about 5.000 - 7.000 men at a minimum. The combined units involved had at least 36 howitzers, 60 heavy mortars, 240 bazookas, 60 anti-aircraft guns, and 44 tanks. They had total air superiority with squadrons from Mostar, Tivat, and Podgorica, and they had three missile boats and two patrol boats deployed. Also three batteries of P-15 surface to surface missiles with an 80-kilometre range were available to them. "The JA plan for the Dubrovnik operation was to launch a two-pronged attack on the region simultaneously from east Herzegovina and from south-western Montenegro. Their first objective was to isolate Dubrovnik and take control of the Croatian coast from the Montenegrin border to the Neretva Valley. They projected that this would take them one week. The second objective was to link up with JA forces coming down the Neretva from Sarajevo and Mostar and to use this enlarged force to move in a north-westerly direction until they joined the SAO Krajina forces move south-easterly. The projected time for this second phase of the operation was another week. These land operations were to be supplemented by naval attacks at the bay of Budim on Peljelac; by air support from bases in Mostar, Podgorica and Tivat; and by artillery and rocket assaults. The total time estimated to achieve their objectives was 15 days." And he goes on in the next paragraph to say the JNA offensives started at the same time from Herzegovina and Montenegro. Does what is recorded there match with your experience of events, Mr. Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final page, for context, that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you go on, is there given a corresponding estimate of the number of personnel defending Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's consistent with what the witness has given, which is why I didn't look for it for contrast, but I'll ask Ms. Bibles to double-check. Yes. Thank you. It was on pages 14 and 15 that he was cross-examined, and I think if you look at the top of page -- if you look at the bottom of page 14 and at the top of page 15, you'll see the reference to 670 soldiers, and the Court will recall the witness's explanation of how that figure matched his own 300 estimate when you take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out the police units. And you'll see on this same page, page 15, the general's explanation for his deployment of the forces available to him. But as to the first point, the 670 soldiers, which we see at the top of page 15, Mr. Simunovic, including ZNG, MUP, and the recently mobilised men, do you accept that figure given here by General Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept it with the explanation that this 607 -- 70 men includes the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that meets Your Honour's concern and I'll ask Ms. Bibles to check if there is any other reference to numbers we should draw to your attention before I close. She says not. In those circumstances, can I draw to the Court's attention a route map -- as a route map through this particular statement, page 19. It's really deployment of his forces, or the forces available to him, starting at page 19, second fresh paragraph: "During the fighting in the east, I lost one of the truck-mounted anti-aircraft guns when it was bombed by an aircraft at Zvekovica. Unfortunately, the crew was killed. I lost the two 88-millimetre cannons at Resnici near Molunat. The improvised firing pins that we had installed on those guns had broken after only a couple of shells were fired. The crew manning the guns tried to get new ones made at the TUP factory, and when they returned to the area, the JA had already taken the location as part of their amphibious landings and the men were captured, as were the guns. "After the area to the east of Dubrovnik had been occupied by the JA and with their advance in the west continuing, I had withdrawn most of my weaponry to the area of the city. I also received a few more weapons that were brought into the city from Sipan, including two more 85-millimetre cannons and two zis guns."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pausing there. Mr. Simunovic, I don't know that you told us about that. Do you know about it? Do you accept it is accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about it, and I do accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he goes on to detail what was available in this way: "In the period between mid-October and the end of December 1991, I had the following heavy weapons in the city of Dubrovnik itself, and placed as indicated: One zis at the end of Babin Kuk." Now, if that map is available, it may help if you're able to -- would you be able, Mr. Simunovic, to point out where these various locations are if we put the map on the projector? More particularly to see whether they're in the old town or not. I'll just read out and you put the map on, please. We can see the map. Right. So three -- one zis at the end of Babin Kuk. Where is that and where is that in relation to the old town, so we can see it?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right up on the north, near Rijeka, the river. Three mortars near the campground at Babin Kuk. Is that the similar sort of area?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Two 85 cannons on Lapad with 48 shells. Lapad, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the registrar suggests we get some initialling or something of that sort to indicate what is what.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could write the letter A - and if that pen isn't strong enough, we'll find you a stronger one - A for the end of Babin Kuk, please. If you could write it on the map, Mr. Simunovic. Just write A for the end of Babin Kuk, B for the campground at Babin Kuk, C for Lapad. The general's statement continues: Two zis near the playing fields below the Hotel Lero. We'll mark that as D, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One zis on the Lapad peninsula west of the Hotel Libertas. Mark that E, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two 23 anti-aircraft guns on Lapad west of the Hotel Lero. Mark that F, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, finally, three 82-millimetre mortars in Bogisica Park west of the Hotel Imperijal. Mark that G, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you accept or challenge the accuracy of that account?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last paragraph on the same page - I'm sorry we don't have the general's map immediately to hand, or if we have, I haven't produced it - the last entry on the same page says: "The only other heavy weapons that were used inside the city of Dubrovnik were the two truck-mounted 20-millimetre anti-aircraft cannons." Do you accept that those two cannons were also deployed, Mr. Simunovic?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannon was 20-millimetre calibre, and I think that one was a machine-gun, a Browning 12.7 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour will see -- Your Honours will see what starts at the top of page 20, but I don't understand the cross-examination, unless I've missed it, to have been specific as to any assertion that there was firing from the old town. But the material is there even if I'm wrong. Just a couple of other questions, I think, from you, please, Mr. Simunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused suggested to you that the residents of Dubrovnik of Serb ethnicity felt themselves to be in jeopardy. Was there, to your knowledge and within your experience, anything happening that could have explained their being in jeopardy?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was happening for them to feel in jeopardy. On the contrary, a part of them took an active part in the defence of Dubrovnik and were members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave an answer dealing with illegally built houses. We haven't explored this in detail before. In a couple of sentences, can you explain, please, the significance of and part in the history played by illegally built houses and their destruction.

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm probably not the right person to be able to explain that in detail, but I am able to say the following: Before the war, I was a manager in a work organisation, a company, in which there were a number of Croats of a different religion, so that there were quite a number of them. Not one of them had their houses destroyed, which means that regardless of the fact that they didn't have building permits for those houses, those houses were not on roads, they were not an obstacle to normal traffic, and I believe those houses are still standing there, though they didn't have a building permit for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any houses destroyed? Was the destruction of houses ever relied upon, either at the time or after the event, as an explanation for the attack that was launched on Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody engaged in that kind of action towards other ethnic groups in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked about two Judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a point. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider that the opposite side is leading the witness in quite an erroneous manner, because he claims that I claimed that there were I don't know what kinds of abuses, and I was in fact quoting exclusively from court documents from the Dubrovnik courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt you. Yes, I know that but he's entitled to cross-examine -- to re-examine, rather, on the material that you examined about. He's entitled to ask questions about that. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked in this very context, Mr. Simunovic, about two Judges, one of whom was called Gajic, and you gave an answer that, because of translation uncertainties, is unclear. You were asked by the accused whether the report of one or other of these Judges would be a document to be accepted. You said as to the first gentleman, which is Judge Gajic, that's not possible. I don't want a long answer, but can you please say this: Are you accepting that what Judge Gajic wrote is something that should be relied upon or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he somebody whose word or report should be relied upon, in your judgement, or not?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my judgement, it is not a credible witness, and what he stated, if he did indeed state it, then a great question mark must be put after the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm not going to explore with you the particular reasons for that view, but I just wanted that clarified. Finally - I think finally - you explained how Damjanovic appeared differently in public from the things that he said in private. Was that a behaviour pattern that Svicevic also revealed, that he said a different approach in public from the approach he took in private?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Svicevic did not behave like General Damjanovic. He considered privately and publicly to follow his orthodox views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can see this on page 9 of your statement. At one stage when asking -- asked by you what they were doing, said he was here to liberate Dubrovnik from the Ustasha and the Kurds; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Svicevic thought I was an Ustasha too. But in our conversations later on when I asked him what he was doing there, he said he had come to free us from ourselves, liberate us from ourselves. And my response to him was that had I been mobilised and sent to Montenegro, for example, or Serbia, I would not have responded to the mobilisation call, and I would have suffered all the consequences probably that are put into place in cases of that kind. He said no, that he was doing it all with full consciousness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, we looked at the material that you've been challenged with about the comparative strength of the various forces. At any time did the forces that you say were defending Dubrovnik take aggressive action against the JNA other than in defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: IVO SIMUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the actions taken by the Croatian army in the area of responsibility of the command of the Dubrovnik municipality were put into effect by defensive operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those conclude my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, two points: In view of the extensive use that has been made of this statement, the Chamber would urge you to use your best efforts to have this witness attend court. Secondly, yesterday I raised the question of the designation of Dubrovnik as a UNESCO protected site. It does not appear to be challenged by the accused. However, in view of the bearing that that designation might have for the Chamber when it comes to assess the events in Dubrovnik at the end of the day, it would be proper, it would seem to me, to have more evidence on the criteria for the designation and the general implications that arise from such designation. It is obviously a matter of some importance. For example, on page 20 of the statement, I see a reference to -- in the first paragraph to that people went to the old town, relying on the belief that because of its status and its historical character, it would never be targeted. So that in view of the importance of that designation, we would like to have more specific evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that a witness already listed to come will be dealing with this on a much more expert basis, and I hope will have the materials to satisfy the Court's concern. Dealing with Your Honour's first point, as I've indicated at an earlier stage, the efforts we were already going to make to have General Marinovic available for cross-examination will be maintained, and I probably will be in a position to report back to you in about two weeks' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ought to deal with exhibiting the marked map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked map will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 326 tab 13.IS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what we're going to do is this: If the witness is available, then of course you'll be able to cross-examine. If not, we will give you the opportunity in due course to make some observations, if you wish, upon the statement since you haven't had the chance to do so. Mr. Simunovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for making it possible for me to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It would convenient, unless there's anything you want to raise, Mr. Nice, to take the break now, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It might be convenient if I deal with something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness go, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to deal with in closed session in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, could I have two minutes in private session before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, perhaps you'd better give the witnesses name or pseudonym, rather, so we may know who it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is the Witness C-013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, SUP Vukovar, did it have a mixed police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Approximately 50/50; fifty per cent were Croats, 50 per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the year 1990, was there increasing ethnic tension both in the town and in the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vukovar town, was it predominantly populated by Croats at that time, the town as such?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the municipality of Vukovar as a whole, what was the ethnic composition there? Was it the same or different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: It was different. 65 per cent were Serbs, approximately, and 30 per cent Croats. Five per cent were the others, other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While in Vukovar, did you receive information that the Serbs and Croats were arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1990, did the Croatian authorities increase the number of police in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, what was -- was there an atmosphere of distrust, of fear within the police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb policemen in Vukovar resign from the police force at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I think that was at the end of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the police -- of the Serb policemen, how many, approximately, did resign? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: All the Serb policemen. About 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around that time, end of March, beginning April 1991, was there anything on TV displayed that disturbed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, about the arming of Croatia, which was organised by General Martin Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which TV station did send it, and was that sent only once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: No, not once, several times. And it was on Television Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fear for the safety of your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the witness to get closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, quite certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please move a little bit closer to the microphone. The interpreters can't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Is this better?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, because of this fear, did you therefore go to a location that was inhabited by Serbs? And what did your family do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did your family do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you what did your family do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: They went with me to the same village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they subsequently leave for Belgrade or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Because of the lack of safety. It was extremely unsafe. One couldn't move around. So I decided they should go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to speak to you about the situation in the village of Bobota. Did the village have a village defence in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this village defence, did these people have weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: They did, but not military weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of this village defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Rade Kresojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a local person, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you who was he. Was he a military person? Was he police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: No. He had a position in Vukovar municipality. I think he was a deputy or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the village -- the village defence did not have military weapons at that time. Did they get military weapons; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. Just around that time, weapons started arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the weapons arrive in Bobota? Can you explain how that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I can. The weapons were brought in from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: All kinds of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific? What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Military weapons. Rifles of various calibres and types, mortars, mines, bombs, and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they got the weapons from Borovo Selo. How did the weapons get to Borovo Selo? Do you know that? Where did the weapons actually originate from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: It came from Serbia, across the Danube.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it crossed the Danube, how was it then distributed? Where did it actually arrive and how was it distributed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: It arrived in trucks. There were warehouses in the village, and then members of the Territorial Defence from the villages outside Borovo Selo came to Borovo Selo and took over the weapons and drove them off to their village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the weapons arrived, did they -- were they in crates or boxes or were they loose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in boxes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any seals or inscriptions on the boxes so that you could see where they originate from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. It was military weapons of the JNA, of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo at that time, was there a Serbian TO and was there -- did they have a headquarters there, or why did they arrive in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Borovo Selo was specific in terms of its territory, that is, it was along the Danube itself, on the banks of the Danube, and it was easiest to cross the Danube and reach Borovo Selo. The other villages were under blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the other side of the river, on the other side of Borovo Selo, is there a Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo, who was the commander at the time, the Serbian TO commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Vukasin Soskocanin, known as Vule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a professional solder or a police person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: No. I think he was a vet in Borovo village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he eventually die, drown in the river in 1991 and do you know when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Around the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: He was replaced by Jovica Vucenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a local person, and if so, what -- did you know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, a local person, and I did know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who organised the transport of the weapons from Serbia to Borovo Selo and then the distribution to the villages? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: The weapons came from a certain Sarac. I don't know his first name. And as I said a moment ago, there were warehouses in the village, and from those warehouses the weapons were distributed to other villages in the region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sarac, what kind of a person was he? To whom was he related? Can you tell us? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I do not know Sarac personally, but I do know from contacts with other people that he is from the state security, either from Novi Sad or from Belgrade. I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we briefly go into private session for just actually two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In beginning of May 1991, did clashes occur in Borovo Selo between the Croatian police and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: The question isn't clear to me. Please, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen on the 1st of May or 2nd of May, 1991, involving Croatian police and the local Serb TO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. On the 2nd of May, the Croatian police stormed the village of Borovo with about 200 or 300 men, and there was shooting, an exchange of fire when several local people were killed as well as some members of the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene in this situation and, if so, in which way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The JNA entered the village, and I can freely say that it assisted the Croatian policemen to pull out of the village, because there was a danger of the conflicts continuing, which would have been disastrous for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this incident on the 2nd of May, 1991, did the JNA stay in the region, and who was then in control of Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA stayed there, and they controlled Borovo Selo throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were any irregular soldiers in Borovo Selo, such as Seselj's White Eagles or the like? I mean around the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I don't know what their name was, but there were some members, and they had Chetnik insignias.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the TO headquarters in Borovo Selo? Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: In the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA also have a military post in Borovo Selo itself and, if so, where was this post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes; close by. Maybe there was some 50 metres dividing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the TO and the JNA cooperate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way? What -- what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Mostly from the TO staff, they went to meetings in the JNA staff or headquarters, and also they would come to the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what -- if there were any briefings and in which way they cooperated? What did it involve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Cooperation consisted of the JNA in the TO headquarters telling them what was going on outside the territory of Borovo Selo and where the guard duty should be reinforced and what things particular attention should be devoted to. I think that was the kind of cooperation between the TO and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the JNA person that the TO had contacts with? Is there any particular person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: At that time, the commander there, I just remember his surname. His surname was Garevski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I think he was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May and June 1991, did politicians come to Borovo Selo and give speeches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. There were several rallies, and I remember the politicians who came. I personally saw Vojislav Seselj, Mihalj Kertes, and Jovan Raskovic also came in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Vojislav Seselj, did you hear him give a speech; and what was the gist of the speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: I did. I was personally present at that rally. Seselj's slogans were the ones that he publicly proclaimed on television on the protection of the Serbian people in the RSK and on the borders that the Serbs should have, should capture, should take control of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the borders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: They are the well-known borders; Karlobag, Virovitica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you also see at that time, that is May, June 1991, a person with the name Jovo Ostojic in Borovo Selo; and if so, who was he and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Jovo several times in Borovo Selo. He wore Chetnik insignia, and I never learned what his role was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a group of men with him that he commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this person and also the group that he commanded eventually leave Borovo Selo; and if so, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-013
utterances.text: Yes. They were there maybe for a total of one month in Borovo Selo, and later on they went to the area of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go now into private session in relation to a meeting that the witness had. It's actually paragraph 9 in the summary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
